land.text: the Kingdom of Portugal and the Algarves with its colonies as the 1908-1910 Cliopatria shape draws them (Cliopatria's Kingdom shape lacks Goa and Timor, which the Republic's first shape adds)

Cliopatria's own Kingdom shape for 1911 (562 km2 at Cabo Verde) is a leftover; the Republic row starts 1911.

correction.text: the Republic's first Cliopatria shape (metropole, Azores, Madeira, Cabo Verde, Guinea, Sao Tome, Angola, Mozambique, Goa and Timor) taken back to the proclamation of 5 October 1910

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: the page gives 'Established: 5 October 1910' but Cliopatria's Portuguese Republic row starts in 1911, and its Kingdom of Portugal shape for 1908-1910 omits Goa (21 cells) and Timor (57 cells) that the Republic's 1911 shape adds. The same land was Portuguese before and after the uprising; this keyframe only moves the start back to 1910. Pages opened: by 3 March 1916 Portugal had seized all German ships at Mormugao in Goa (Portugal in World War I) and the campaigns page says 'Timor was occupied and pacified between 1894 and 1912', so both belong to the Republic's land.

1.965 M km2 (6,763 cells: Angola 3,538, Mozambique 2,673, Guinea 131, mainland Portugal 320, Goa 21, Timor 57, Cabo Verde 11, Azores 6, Madeira 4, Sao Tome 2). The infobox of the First Portuguese Republic gives no area. The Angola page gives 1,246,700 km2 (undated); Cliopatria's Angola in 1911-1913 is 3,538 cells, about 0.89 M km2 at 252.9 km2 a cell (ratio 0.72, within the factor of two), because it leaves out Cuando Cubango (all but 6 of its 680 cells) and the east of Moxico (205 cells), which the 1914 shape adds. The pages opened do not say when those lands became Portuguese in fact (see the 1914 ledger event); Cunene is drawn Portuguese from 1911 although the Cuanhama there were beaten only in 1915. Cliopatria draws modern-border Mozambique, so the Kionga Triangle (German until 1919) is inside this shape. Unverified beyond that: page budget.

1,965,602 km2: +562 km2 over 1911, the Cabo Verde cells that Cliopatria's Kingdom of Portugal row carries alone in 1911 (562 km2, 6 cells) and the Republic row takes over in 1912; one cell at Maio differs. A bookkeeping move, not an event: the Portugal in World War I page shows Cabo Verde Portuguese (eight German ships seized at Sao Vicente on 25 February 1916). Unverified: page budget.

2.202 M km2: +236,000 km2 (810 cells) over 1913, all in south-east Angola: Cuando Cubango (598 cells) and Moxico (205 cells), lon 17.5-23 E, lat 13.2-18 S. No page opened dates this step. The campaigns page has German forces attacking the Cuangar fort on 31 October 1914, so a Portuguese post stood on the Cubango by then; its Moxico, Cuando Cubango and Cuando entries are 'not on the page'. Recorded as a confidence-1 gain from nobody in 1914. Angola is now 4,348 cells, about 1.10 M km2, ratio 0.88 to the page's 1,246,700 km2 (undated). From December 1914 to July 1915 the Germans held the Humbe region (ledger occupation events), which the shape does not show.

2,201,913 km2: +140 km2 over 1914, two cells added and two removed near 21.7-23.1 E, 17-18 S (the Angola-Namibia-Zambia corner); no page opened mentions a change there, so it is treated as a redraw (unverified: page budget). The Kionga Triangle, 'occupied on 10 April 1916', is not a change in this shape: Cliopatria's modern-border Mozambique already contains it, so the occupation and the 1919 cession are in the ledger only.

correction.text: the 1917 shape kept whole in 1918: Portuguese Mozambique was not detached; the German column's presence is the hatched occupation of the ledger (November 1917 to August 1918), not a loss of land

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria cuts 827 cells (242,000 km2, leaving 1.959 M km2) out of northern Mozambique for 1918: Cabo Delgado (259 of 266 cells), Niassa (406 of 436), 116 cells of Zambezia and 31 of Nampula. The page: 'on 23 November, Lettow-Vorbeck crossed into Mozambique to plunder supplies from Portuguese garrisons', the Germans 'marched through Mozambique in caravans ... for nine months', 'returned to German East Africa and crossed into Rhodesia in August 1918'. No page says that the Germans took over administration or that any land changed owner, and the Portugal in World War I page has Portuguese Mozambique still the colony after 'July: The German force ... captured Namacurra'. The cut is therefore drawn as occupation, not as a loss, and 1918 reverts to the 1917 shape.

2,201,913 km2, the 1916-1917 shape back whole after the German column left Mozambique in August 1918 (page) and Lettow-Vorbeck surrendered at Abercorn on 25 November 1918. Cliopatria's one-cell difference at 35.8 E, 15.7 S in 1918 is not explained by any page.

Identical to 1919-1923 (2,201,913 km2, 7,574 cells); no territorial change in 1919-1926 on any page opened. Estado Novo's 1926 shape is the same cells. The Angola page adds that the Cabinda territory 'became incorporated into the larger colony' sometime in the 1920s, which Cliopatria draws as Portuguese throughout.

correction.text: the 1925 shape carried to the coup of 28 May 1926 (the page: 'Disestablished: 29 May 1926')

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: the Republic ended in May 1926 (28 May coup, military dictatorship), but Cliopatria's Portuguese Republic row ends 1925 and its Estado Novo row begins 1926 on identical cells. The land does not change hands; if the compiler cannot overlap the two rows in 1926 it should hand over at the start of 1926.

region.text: the republican uprising of 5 October 1910 that overthrew King Manuel II: the metropole, Lisbon at its head, with the colonies of the Kingdom carried over

ledger.note: 1910: the republican uprising of 5 October overthrows King Manuel II and Portugal becomes a republic. Infobox 'Established: 5 October 1910'; 'Preceded by: Kingdom of Portugal and the Algarves'; capital Lisbon. The page names only Mozambique among the colonies, so the whole Cliopatria shape (Africa, Asia, Atlantic islands) rests on the Kingdom's holdings carried over.

region.text: Cuando Cubango and the east of Moxico, the south-east corner Cliopatria adds to Portuguese Angola in 1914

ledger.note: 1914: south-east Angola enters the Portuguese map. Page silent on the date: Cuando Cubango and Moxico are 'not on the page'; the step is Cliopatria's (810 cells, 598 in Cuando Cubango and 205 in Moxico); the page shows the Cuangar fort attacked by German forces on 31 October 1914, a post on the Cubango by then. Treaty frontiers (the 1905 award on the Barotseland frontier, Portuguese Angola page) pre-date it, so the land was claimed earlier.

region.text: the Humbe region around Naulila (Cunene Province is the proxy; the page names Humbe and Naulila)

ledger.note: 1914: Germans take Naulila and the Humbe region. 'the Cuangar fort was attacked by German forces on 31 October 1914'; 'The same happened at the fort of Naulila on 18 December, where 69 Portuguese were killed and 36 taken prisoner'; the Angola page: the Germans 'captured Naulila, forcing the Portuguese to withdraw from the Humbe region'. Owner's record: German South West Africa forces occupy Portuguese land; hatched, no change of owner.

region.text: the Humbe region around Naulila (Cunene Province is the proxy; the page names Humbe and Naulila)

ledger.note: 1915: the Portuguese retake Humbe. 'On 7 July 1915, Portuguese forces reoccupied Humbe, encountering no resistance'; two days later the German force in South West Africa surrendered to General Botha (9 July). Reviewer eu-20-o: confidence 2, the pages name Humbe, not Cunene (a proxy), and neither says German troops held Humbe after Naulila (the campaigns page: Alves Rocadas 'ordered a withdrawal from southern Angola' and the Ovambo revolted).

region.text: the Cuanhama kingdom around its capital Ondjiva

ledger.note: 1915: General Pereira d'Eca's column fights the Cuanhama. He 'landed in Angola in March 1915'; the Cuamato fort was reoccupied on 15 August and the Battle of Mongua was fought on 18-20 August (the page gives the days; the year follows the landing; the extract read names no side at Mongua). The Cuanhama kingdom of Mandume is a state without a dossier; Cliopatria draws Cunene Portuguese throughout.

region.text: the Cuanhama kingdom around its capital Ondjiva

ledger.note: 1915: the Portuguese take Ondjiva. 'On 4 September, Pereira d'Eca occupied Ondjiva, capital of the Cuanhama kingdom, without resistance'; the page adds that peace 'would last for more than 40 years after Mandume's death in 1917', so some resistance outlived the capital's fall.

region.text: the Kionga Triangle, German East Africa's strip south of the Rovuma mouth

ledger.note: 10 April 1916: Portugal occupies the Kionga Triangle. 'Portugal occupied the Kionga Triangle on 10 April 1916'; the Portugal in World War I page has Kionga 'occupied since 1894' and a 1914 force 'tasked with recapturing the Kionga Triangle from the Germans'. This state is the occupier; the owner is German East Africa (german-africa).

region.text: northern Mozambique, the land Lettow-Vorbeck's column marched through after crossing into Mozambique (the pages name Ngomano and Namacurra; the extent follows Cliopatria's 1918 cut: Cabo Delgado, Niassa and parts of Nampula and Zambezia)

ledger.note: November 1917: Lettow-Vorbeck's German column enters Mozambique. 'on 23 November, Lettow-Vorbeck crossed into Mozambique to plunder supplies from Portuguese garrisons' (the page's other sentence puts the entry in November 1917); the Portuguese garrison was routed at Ngomano. Portugal in World War I: 'July: The German force under General Lettow-Vorbeck captured Namacurra'. Owner's record: German forces occupy Portuguese land; hatched, no change of owner. The region is Cliopatria's 1918 cut, my reading.

region.text: northern Mozambique, the land Lettow-Vorbeck's column marched through after crossing into Mozambique (the pages name Ngomano and Namacurra; the extent follows Cliopatria's 1918 cut: Cabo Delgado, Niassa and parts of Nampula and Zambezia)

ledger.note: August 1918: the German column leaves Portuguese Mozambique. 'The Germans returned to German East Africa and crossed into Rhodesia in August 1918'; Lettow-Vorbeck offered his surrender at Abercorn at 11:00 on 25 November 1918, after 'nine months' marching through Mozambique.

region.text: the Kionga Triangle, German East Africa's strip south of the Rovuma mouth

ledger.note: 1919: the Kionga occupation becomes ownership. The page: 'In the Treaty of Versailles, Germany ceded the port of Kionga, associated with German East Africa, to Portugal'; neither the year nor the day is in the sentence I read, and the Peace Conference entry is dated 'January 19'. The year 1919 is my bridging (treaty of the Paris peace after the 11 November 1918 armistice). Reviewer eu-20-o: dated by the Portuguese Mozambique page, 'on 28 June 1919, the Treaty of Versailles transferred the Kionga Triangle, a 1,000 km2 (390 sq mi) territory south of the Rovuma River from German East Africa to Mozambique'.

region.text: the Kionga Triangle, German East Africa's strip south of the Rovuma mouth

ledger.note: 1919: the Kionga Triangle is ceded to Portugal at Versailles. 'This was the only territory gained by Portugal for taking part in World War I on the side of the victorious Allies.' Cliopatria's Mozambique already contains the triangle, so the shape does not change; year bridged as for the occupation_end. Reviewer eu-20-o: dated by the Portuguese Mozambique page, 'on 28 June 1919, the Treaty of Versailles transferred the Kionga Triangle, a 1,000 km2 (390 sq mi) territory south of the Rovuma River from German East Africa to Mozambique'.

region.text: the whole Republic, metropole and colonies, passing intact to the military dictatorship (Cliopatria's Estado Novo)

ledger.note: 28 May 1926: a coup d'etat by the armed forces ends the First Republic. The page: 'Disestablished: 29 May 1926', 'the 28 May 1926 coup d'etat'; it led to a military dictatorship called Ditadura Nacional. The metropole and the colonies pass unchanged to the dictatorship (Cliopatria: Estado Novo from 1926).

wars.name: Portugal in World War I
wars.outcome: Allied victory; Portugal seized German ships on 23-25 February 1916, Germany declared war on 9 March 1916 and Austria-Hungary on 15 March; the armistice was 11 November 1918. Kionga was Portugal's only territorial gain. Portugal sent about 12,000 men to France (First Portuguese Republic page).
wars.note: The African fronts that moved land are the four wars below. Timeline in the page: Three ships sunk at Funchal on 3 December 1916, Ponta Delgada bombarded on 4 July 1917.

wars.name: German-Portuguese clashes in southern Angola (Naulila)

zones.text: the Humbe region around Naulila (Cunene Province is the proxy; the page names Humbe and Naulila)

wars.outcome: German attacks at Cuangar (31 October 1914) and Naulila (18 December 1914) drive the Portuguese from the Humbe region; Pereira d'Eca lands in March 1915, reoccupies Humbe on 7 July 1915 and the German force in South West Africa surrenders to Botha on 9 July.
wars.note: The Portuguese Angola page puts the Germans' return and capture of Naulila in December and says the population of southern Angola fell by at least a quarter during the war.

wars.name: Cuanhama campaign of 1915

zones.text: the Cuanhama kingdom around its capital Ondjiva

wars.outcome: Portuguese win: the Cuamato fort reoccupied 15 August, the Battle of Mongua 18-20 August, Ondjiva occupied without resistance on 4 September 1915; Mandume dies in 1917.
wars.note: Cliopatria draws Cunene Portuguese since 1911; the contest is an overlay on land the shape already gives to Portugal.

wars.name: Kionga Triangle occupation

zones.text: the Kionga Triangle, German East Africa's strip south of the Rovuma mouth

wars.outcome: Portugal occupies the triangle on 10 April 1916; the Treaty of Versailles cedes Kionga to Portugal on 28 June 1919 (Portuguese Mozambique page).
wars.note: Fighting is not described on the pages opened; the Portugal in World War I page says only that a force was tasked to recapture it in 1914.

wars.name: German invasion of Portuguese Mozambique

zones.text: northern Mozambique, the land Lettow-Vorbeck's column marched through after crossing into Mozambique (the pages name Ngomano and Namacurra; the extent follows Cliopatria's 1918 cut: Cabo Delgado, Niassa and parts of Nampula and Zambezia)

wars.outcome: Lettow-Vorbeck crosses into Mozambique on 23 November 1917, routs the garrison at Ngomano, lives off Portuguese supplies for nine months, takes Namacurra in July 1918 and returns to German East Africa in August 1918; no land changes owner.
wars.note: Zone = Cliopatria's 1918 cut; the pages name only Ngomano and Namacurra.

wars.name: Barue uprising
wars.outcome: The page gives no result: 'Also in 1917, the Barue uprising took place and while it lasted, the Germans invaded Mozambique with 300 soldiers and 1,700 askari'.
wars.note: The 1918 Barue events are 'not on the page'.

wars.name: Portuguese campaigns of pacification and occupation, 1910-1915 phase
belligerents: local polities of Angola, Mozambique, Guinea and Timor
wars.outcome: Angola: Cassai reached and the north-east complete in 1912, the Cuanhama beaten in 1915, the south 'only pacified in 1926'. Mozambique: Angoche conquered 1910, Macua and Makonde between the Mogabo and Messalo pacified 1909-1910, interior occupation concluded 1908-1912, Namarrais pacified 1913. Guinea: mainland 'fully occupied by 1915'. Timor: 'occupied and pacified between 1894 and 1912'.
wars.note: Zones empty: Cliopatria draws all of these lands Portuguese from 1911, so no border moves between keyframes; they show how soft the interior frontiers were.

certainty.note: Mainland Portugal and the colonies' treaty frontiers (the Angola page: the Barotseland frontier by the 1905 award of the King of Italy; borders with other powers fixed during the Scramble) are sharp on paper. Soft in fact, and drawn from Cliopatria cells: the interior of Angola (south 'only pacified in 1926'; the Cuanhama until 1915; the south-east not dated), Guinea until 1915, Timor until 1912, the Kionga Triangle (a German strip to 1919) and the German-held cut of 1917-1918.

notes: Cliopatria row 'Portuguese Republic' (1911-1925, 7 shapes) is one state; the dossier starts it on 5 October 1910 and ends it on 28 May 1926 (First Portuguese Republic page) with two new keyframes (1910, 1926) on the same cells. The wikipedia field says 'First Portuguese Republic'; Cliopatria's own field says 'Portugal' (the country article). Page budget (5 pages for 7 shapes) was spent on the republic's page, the Angola page, the campaigns page and the two World War I pages. Not settled: (1) why Cliopatria adds Cuando Cubango and east Moxico only in 1914 (810 cells); no page opened dates it, the ledger gain is confidence 1, and the 1911-1913 shapes arguably under-draw Angola given the 1905 award; a gap-filler should open 'Cuando Cubango Province' and 'Moxico Province'. (2) The Kionga cession year (1919) is bridged; af-08's portuguese-mozambique dossier cites a 28 June 1919 date from a page I did not open. (3) Timor, Macau, Goa, Guinea and Sao Tome have no dated event here; the Timor frontier with the Dutch part is not researched (page budget). Cliopatria has no shape for Macau and a 21-cell Goa, 57-cell Timor, 131-cell Guinea and 2-cell Sao Tome, all inherited by the 1911 shape. Occupation events: schema direction used = the dossier state is the occupier; for German occupations of Portuguese land (Humbe 1914-1915, Mozambique 1917-1918) the owner's record is written, with the German side as counterpart, as in the Tang example; each note says who is who. The 1918 Cliopatria cut is read as occupation, not loss. Region names the gazetteer may lack: the Kionga Triangle (a 15 km radius is used), Namacurra (named in notes only), Humbe and Naulila (Cunene Province is the proxy). Counterparts without a dossier: the Cuanhama kingdom of Mandume (1915 contest, string 'Cuanhama kingdom'); the successor row Estado Novo belongs to another group; the page names the Ditadura Nacional as successor but no Cliopatria row exists for it. Reviewer eu-20-o (2026-10-31): the Kionga cession is dated 28 June 1919 from the Portuguese Mozambique page (/ledger/9-10); /ledger/3 lowered to confidence 2; portuguese-empire added as a predecessor for Goa and Timor.
